name: Operating Expense
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Running the Machine: What It Actually Costs to Keep a Blockchain Alive
lesson.summary: Operating expense is the recurring cost of keeping a blockchain-based system running, folding together computational cost and transaction cost, and unlike conventional software it tends to scale roughly linearly with how much an application is actually used.
lesson.body:
Operating expense is the broader category that computational cost and transaction cost both feed into: the ongoing, recurring costs of actually running a blockchain-based system in production, as opposed to the one-time cost of building it. For a business evaluating whether to use blockchain technology, this is usually the number that matters most, because a system that is elegant on paper but expensive to keep running day after day will struggle to justify itself against a conventional database that does the same job for a fraction of the ongoing cost. Operating expense pulls together electricity and hardware for anyone running nodes or mining, the transaction fees paid every time the system needs to write new data, and the staffing and monitoring needed to keep everything functioning correctly.

The two prior concepts show up here as direct line items. Computational cost, the mining or validating expense that secures the network, is borne either directly, if the business runs its own mining or validating infrastructure, or indirectly, since a network's overall computational cost influences the fees users pay to transact on it. Transaction cost then shows up explicitly every time the business's application writes data to the chain: registering a record, transferring an asset, or executing a smart contract function. A supply chain company that logs a milestone for every shipment on a public blockchain is not paying once, it is paying a transaction fee for every single shipment, every single time, which means the operating expense scales directly with usage rather than shrinking through economies of scale the way it might on a company-owned server.

This distinguishes blockchain operating expense from traditional software in a way that matters for planning. A conventional web application's marginal cost of serving one more request is close to zero once the servers are running, so a company can grow usage substantially before operating expenses climb meaningfully. A blockchain application, in contrast, has a marginal cost attached to nearly every meaningful action, since each one is a transaction with its own fee, so operating expense tends to scale roughly linearly, or worse during periods of network congestion, with how much the application is actually used. A company that expected blockchain to lower its long-run costs can discover the opposite: the more successful the application becomes, the more it costs to keep running, in direct proportion to its own success.

Recognizing operating expense as a distinct, ongoing category, rather than folding it into the one-time cost of building the system, is what separates a realistic blockchain proposal from an overly optimistic one. It is also the natural bridge to infrastructure cost, discussed next, which covers the other major recurring expense: the hardware and network resources required simply to run the nodes that participate in the blockchain at all, independent of any specific transaction.
